catalog_locator: p. 6 and p. 9, section 2.1 'Phonological structure of noun and verb roots' (table (2) lists 'Primary stress' under sigma-1)
catalog_quote: The first root syllable in Mpyemo is prominent. Contrast is at its maximum in the first root syllable and decreases as one moves rightwards. … The first root syllable has a special prominence, bearing stress and displaying the full inventory of phonemic contrasts, except for three marginal phonemes, (/ŋ, h, ɾ/). … Additionally, the C1 position is where primary stress is located.

tone_statements.quote: Le mpyemo comporte deux tons sous-jacents : le ton haut (H) et le ton bas (B). Le ton super-haut (sH) est le résultat de règles tonologiques.
tone_statements.translation: Mpyemo has two underlying tones: the high tone (H) and the low tone (B). The super-high tone (sH) is the result of tonological rules.

tone_statements.citation: Festen, Bradley D. 2018. Phonological Sketch of the Mpyemo Language. Bangui: ACATBA (Association Centrafricaine pour la Traduction de la Bible et l'Alphabétisation) & SIL International, SIL Central African Republic Service Group, November 2018. iv + 100 pp. (section 4 'Tone', pp. 26-31; Appendix B c. 1000-item tone-marked wordlist). CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
tone_statements.quote: Mpyemo has three phonetic pitch levels, but only two underlying tone heights: high and low. Two of the phonetic pitch levels are produced by unchanged high and low tones. The third is generated by a high tone raising (HTR) rule, where a high tone is raised to the “super-high” level when followed by a low tone. In the middle of an utterance, the triggering low tone can be either associated or floating, but in the utterance-final position, the low must be associated in order to trigger HTR.
tone_statements.locator: p. 27, section 4 'Tone' (section heading at foot of p. 26)
tone_statements.n_tones: 2 underlying (H, L); 3 surface levels (L, H, super-high via HTR)

Acoustic study (vowels, long vowels, implosives, labialised velars, prenasalised stops) of the Nola (CAR) variety, one main informant; tone marked impressionistically as high/low (p. 166 fn. 4); notes long vowels 'tended to have a lower pitch' (p. 168) and that 'a phonetically long vowel could have a different tone within it' (p. 169); F0 of word-initial nasal compared with prefix /a/ (p. 176). No word on accent/stress. downloaded from GUPEA (handle 2077/84756) via the DSpace REST API.
